abstract: ABSTRACT Plant cell culture (PCC) presents a promising and sustainable alternative to traditional agricultural methods for producing specialty bioactive compounds. However, its widespread industrial application has been hindered by challenges such as low yields, cell line instability and inconsistent product quality. engineering biology (EB) offers a powerful toolkit to overcome these limitations by systematically improving plant cell lines. This review focuses on the application of EB principles to enhance PCC for the production of high‐value bioactives from an industry‐oriented perspective. We explore three core pillars of the EB toolkit: (1) Multiomics and in silico design, which leverage comprehensive data integration and predictive modelling for rational target identification; (2) gene manipulation and pathway bioengineering, encompassing precise genome editing (e.g., CRISPR/Cas), synthetic gene circuits and directed evolution for targeted metabolic reprogramming and (3) biosensors for high‐throughput screening and real‐time monitoring, enabling rapid testing and optimisation of engineered cell lines. The synergistic integration of these tools within the iterative design‐build‐test‐learn (DBTL) cycle is highlighted as a key strategy for accelerating strain improvement. Ultimately, the convergence of these EB approaches is transforming PCC into a robust platform for producing pharmaceuticals, functional foods and green chemicals, contributing to a biobased economy with a minimal ecological footprint.
body:
1
Introduction
Plant‐derived bioactive compounds, such as pharmaceuticals, nutraceuticals and cosmetic ingredients, are traditionally obtained by cultivating or wild‐harvesting plants [
1
,
2
,
3
]. These methods often suffer from low yields, significant environmental impact and inconsistent supply [
1
,
4
]. Plant cell culture (PCC) offers a sustainable in vitro production platform for valuable secondary metabolites under controlled conditions [
5
].
PCC gained prominence with early successes, such as shikonin from
Lithospermum erythrorhizon
[
6
] and the anticancer drug paclitaxel from
Taxus
sp. [
7
], both produced at industrial scale via plant cell fermentation [
8
]. Notably, large bioreactors, up to 75,000 L, were used in Germany for paclitaxel production [
9
]. Compared to field cultivation or wild harvest, plant cell cultures provide year‐round, climate‐independent production under sterile conditions [
10
,
11
]. This alleviates pressure on endangered plants [
12
,
13
] and reduces the environmental footprint of sourcing bioactive compounds [
14
,
15
]. Furthermore, in vitro production enables consistent quality under good manufacturing practice (GMP) control [
16
]. Research has demonstrated that PCC‐derived products can meet the same purity and efficacy standards as plant‐extracted ones. For instance, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved PCC‐derived paclitaxel following demonstration of its equivalency to the natural source [
11
].
Despite these advantages, only a few bioactive compounds have been commercialised via PCC to date [
17
]. Many other valuable metabolites remain underexploited because yields and consistency from cell cultures have often been too low to compete effectively with chemical synthesis or agricultural sourcing [
18
,
19
]. Modern engineering biology (EB) approaches are making a critical difference here [
20
,
21
,
22
]. By systematically improving the cell line (generating new strains), EB can unlock significantly more of PCC's potential. Recent advances in EB, including multiomics analysis, precise gene editing (e.g., CRISPR) and sophisticated synthetic biology tools, are reinvigorating PCC as a platform for sustainable bioactive production. These tools enable the rational engineering of ‘plant cell factories’ for higher productivity, mirroring the strain improvements that revolutionised microbial fermentations [
5
,
23
].
This review adopts an industry‐focused perspective on applying the EB toolkit to plant cell cultures for strain improvement. We outline strategies that can translate PCCs into commercially viable, sustainable factories for specialty bioactives.
2
Plant Cell Culture: Benefits and Challenges
PCC gained prominence due to difficulties in synthesising complex metabolites chemically and challenges in extracting them in sufficient abundance from wild plants. Although microbial platforms offer rapid growth and easier scalability, PCC remains essential for compounds requiring complex plant‐specific biochemical pathways.
PCC leverages totipotency, a characteristic allowing many plant cells to revert to an undifferentiated state and regenerate into an entire plant under appropriate conditions [
24
]. It involves cultivating plant cells in tightly controlled sterile environments using defined nutrient media [
25
,
26
,
27
,
28
].
Generally, PCC is established by surface‐sterilising a healthy explant and inducing the formation of callus, an unorganised mass of undifferentiated cells, on a solid medium containing macronutrients, micronutrients, a carbon source and hormones [
29
,
30
]. Plant cell suspensions are then established by transferring friable callus into liquid medium with agitation, allowing cells derived from the callus to proliferate as single cells or small aggregates [
29
,
31
].
Compared to wild harvesting or agricultural production, PCC offers significant advantages in generating high‐value specialty metabolites. It offers the potential for controlled and consistent production, independent of environmental variables [
12
] and promotes sustainability and conservation by reducing pressure on wild plants and potentially lowering resource consumption [
14
,
15
,
32
].
As higher eukaryotes, plant cells can perform complex post‐translational modifications absent from simpler microbial production platforms, such as glycosylation, as in the example of taliglucerase alfa (Elelyso), an FDA‐approved enzyme‐replacement therapy for Gaucher disease [
33
,
34
,
35
]. Meanwhile, hairy root cultures, a variant of PCC induced by transformation of roots with
Rhizobium rhizogenes
, often exhibit stable high‐level metabolite production similar to the parent plant and grow rapidly in hormone‐free medium [
36
,
37
]. T
he use of hormone‐free medium is of note because of long‐running concerns about the human health impact of exposure to hormones, such as the auxins 2,4‐dichlorophenoxyacetic acid and 1‐naphthaleneacetic acid, used to maintain cultured plant cells in an undifferentiated state
[
38
,
39
]
. These concerns necessitate the removal of such hormones from PCC products, which can increase the complexity, and with it the cost, of downstream product recovery processes. Auxins may also cause somaclonal variation, which can result in a cell line losing its commercially attractive traits
[
40
]
. In effect, this can reduce both the production lifetime of a cell culture line and the production scale that can be reached before productivity declines.
The capacity of PCC to produce secondary metabolites can be enhanced via elicitation [
41
,
42
]. Elicitors are factors that mimic stress conditions, triggering plant defence signalling and the accumulation of defence‐associated secondary metabolites [
42
]. Elicitors can be biotic (e.g., chitosan [
43
,
44
], methyl jasmonate [
45
], salicylic acid [
46
] and proline [
47
]) or abiotic (e.g., ozone [
48
] and copper [
49
]). The success of elicitation heavily depends on the choice of elicitor, its concentration, the timing and duration of exposure, and the specific plant cell line's innate responsiveness.
PCC has been used to produce high‐value bioactives commercially [
50
]. For instance, food additives, such as teupolioside and echinacoside, have been produced using
Ajuga reptans
L. and
Echinacea angustifolia
DC. cell suspensions [
51
], water extracts from
Symphytum officinale
L. and
Saponaria pumila
L. callus have been used in the cosmetics industry [
17
] and
Quillaja saponaria
cell suspensions have been used to produce the vaccine adjuvant QS‐21 [
52
].
Despite the advantages of PCC, it still faces several hurdles that have restricted industrial deployment. Productivity inconsistency is one such hurdle. For example, in
Taxus
PCC, paclitaxel yield varied approximately 6.9‐fold across multiple generations over a 6‐month period [
53
]. Furthermore, general instability in the yield of both specialised metabolites (e.g., paclitaxel) and nonspecialised metabolites (e.g., flavonoids and phenolic compounds) across multiple passages has been observed in
Taxus
cultures [
54
]. Cell line heterogeneity and genetic instability over the prolonged culture periods required for scale‐up and production are inherent to this challenge. In
Catharanthus roseus
cell culture, only about 10% of cells accumulate anthocyanins due to heterogeneity [
55
]. Another study found that selected
C. roseus
cell lines with high alkaloid productivity lost 50% of their production capacity within a year of establishment [
56
], posing a major obstacle for scaled‐up production.
Low volumetric yield also remains a dominant economic barrier for most specialty metabolite PCC programs, particularly in comparison to bacterial and yeast systems [
57
]. Substantial improvements to product titres are typically needed to achieve economic viability, and the product cost reductions achieved by such improvements may appear disappointingly small relative to the improvement in product titres. For instance, an early technoeconomic model indicated that a tenfold increase in cellular yield of ajmalicine from
C. roseus
cell cultures would be required to reduce the costs of producing 30,000 kg of ajmalicine by PCC from an uncompetitive $1500/kg to a commercially feasible $430/kg [
58
]. Accordingly, only a few plant‐derived molecules (notably shikonin, paclitaxel and berberine) have reached the truly cost‐competitive yields required for full commercialisation via PCC [
57
,
59
].
Traditionally, achieving improvements to product titres has involved extensive screening and selection: isolating superior clones from many initial explants or mutagenised cells, often derived from elite donor plants, followed by optimising media and cultivation conditions [
60
,
61
,
62
]. Classic successes using this approach include an 19‐fold increase in camptothecin yields from
Ophiorrhiza mungos
L. [
63
], a 13‐fold increase in shikonin derivatives yield from
Lithospermum erythrorhizon
[
6
,
64
] and a 13.6‐fold increase in alkaloid yields from
Catharanthus roseus
[
56
]. However, achieving extreme strain performance through these traditional methods is time‐consuming, resource‐intensive and often yields only limited success.
In summary, achieving industrial viability with PCC requires stable, high‐yielding cell lines for the target compound. To capture market opportunities efficiently and rapidly, improving the strain improvement process is imperative, but conventional approaches to achieving this are time and resource intensive and are not always sufficient on their own. In this context, engineering biology approaches play a pivotal and transformative role (Figure
1
).
FIGURE 1
A comparison of traditional and engineering biology workflows for the development of plant cell production lines. Developing a production cell line begins by using explants to generate callus cultures, which are then adapted into liquid suspension cultures. High‐performing cell lines are identified through screening and selection from the heterogeneous cultures. Traditionally, bioprocess improvement and scale‐up to bioreactors is then undertaken using the highest performing cell lines (A). The initial steps are the same when incorporating engineering biology principles, but, following selection, the cell line itself undergoes an improvement phase driven by the iterative design‐build‐test‐learn (DBTL) cycle. This allows for rational engineering of the cells for enhanced productivity or other desired traits before bioprocess improvement and scaled production.
3
Engineering Biology Toolkit for Strain Improvement
Engineering biology (EB) offers a suite of powerful tools and rational design strategies to overcome the inherent limitations of traditional methods of PCC strain and process improvement. The central aim is to systematically engineer ‘plant cell factories’ to have enhanced productivity of desired bioactive compounds, improved genetic and phenotypic stability and potentially the capacity to synthesise novel molecules. Core EB tools include multiomics technologies, gene‐editing tools, synthetic biology approaches for pathway and circuit design and targeted metabolic engineering, all tailored for the unique context of plant cell systems. A recurring theme is the synergistic application of these tools, often within an iterative design‐build‐test‐learn (DBTL) framework, to achieve complex engineering goals [
65
].
3.1
Multi‐Omics Analysis and In Silico Design
Systematic improvement of plant cell strains requires a deep understanding of their inherent biological complexity, increasingly achieved by integrating multiomics technologies with sophisticated in silico design strategies [
66
]. Paired multiomics workflows, which encompass combinations of genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, fluxomics and phenomics, collect multiple data layers from the same biological replicates. This holistic approach is critical for uncovering causal gene‐metabolite relationships that might not be apparent from single omics studies [
66
,
67
]. For instance, the discovery of the falcarindiol biosynthetic pathway in tomato was facilitated by correlating time‐resolved metabolite and transcript data across seven different conditions [
66
,
68
,
69
,
70
]. Furthermore, advancements in single‐cell multiomics, such as coupling single‐cell RNA‐sequencing with high‐throughput single‐cell mass spectrometry, have illuminated how processes, such as monoterpene indole alkaloid biosynthesis, are partitioned among distinct cell types in
Catharanthus roseus
leaves, leading to the identification of a previously unknown reductase enzyme in the pathway [
71
]. For PCC specifically, a systems‐level study in
Taxus
suspension cultures showed that methyl jasmonate increases paclitaxel yet imposes growth costs, with phenylpropanoid–taxane flux competition, generation‐to‐generation variability and aggregate‐size‐driven heterogeneity all contributing to titre spread [
54
].
Leveraging these rich datasets is significantly advanced by their integration into pan‐genome frameworks [
72
]. Comparing multiple plant accessions or independently derived cell lines allows pan‐genome analysis to distinguish core metabolic genes present in all accessions from accessory loci present in only a subset of accessions. The presence or absence of accessory loci often explains quantitative differences in metabolite yields [
73
,
74
]. Biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), responsible for many specialised metabolites, are frequently found within this accessory genome. For example, comparative genomics and coexpression mining revealed
DGC7
, a rice gene cluster on chromosome 7 for the synthesis of the defence diterpenoid 5,10‐diketo‐casbene, present in
Oryza japonica
but absent in
Oryza indica
cultivars [
75
]. Large‐scale public datasets, such as the 1000‐Plants (1KP) transcriptome project [
73
] and the expanding repository of over 1000 assembled plant genomes (including draft and reference genome), are invaluable resources [
76
].
These pan‐genome datasets fuel machine learning models that predict which accessory genes or variants are likely to drive high metabolite titres [
74
], enabling directed approaches, such as targeted CRISPR‐mediated knock‐ins, rather than relying solely on extensive untargeted screening [
77
]. An example is seen in Brassicaceae, where genome mining across 55 sequenced genomes identified 21 high‐confidence, colocalised prenyltransferase‐terpene synthase (PT‐TPS) gene pairs. Subsequent transient expression of seven representative TPS genes from
Arabidopsis, Capsella
and
Brassica
in
Nicotiana benthamiana
confirmed their sesterterpene‐synthase activity and led to the identification of several previously uncharacterised molecular scaffolds, including (‐)‐variculatriene A and (‐)‐aleurodiscalene A [
78
]. Although pan‐genome resources richly enumerate allelic and structural variation, they are largely built from whole plants and field/organ tissues (e.g., tomato, rice and
Brassica napus
pan‐genomes), not from dedifferentiated production cultures under bioprocess conditions [
79
,
80
,
81
]. In contrast, plant cell cultures (callus/suspension) occupy distinct transcriptional, metabolic and phytohormone states relative to their source organs, which makes the relevance of organ‐level genotype–phenotype inferences to PCC [
82
]. Moreover, in vitro cultivation itself introduces divergence (somaclonal/epigenetic variation), meaning production lines may differ from the donor genotypes represented in pan‐genomes [
83
,
84
]. Consequently, pan‐genome alleles often do not map 1:1 to culture performance without culture‐context validation. A practical bridge is to use pan‐genomes to narrow the genetic space, then build line‐specific culture‐phase multiomics atlases (e.g., paired time‐series metabolomics + transcriptomics of the same culture) under the actual production regimen to prioritise and verify targets for PCC.
The in silico design phase relies heavily on computational tools, particularly genome‐scale metabolic models (GEMs). Constructed from genomic and biochemical information (often from reference or pan‐genome assemblies), GEMs mathematically represent an organism's entire metabolic network as reported in AraGem [
85
]. To enhance predictive accuracy, these models may be parameterised with experimental data (e.g.,
13
C‐metabolic flux analysis [
86
]) and constrained by transcriptomic [
87
] and proteomic data [
88
]. This refined computational framework allows in silico prediction of the metabolic consequences of genetic modifications (e.g., gene knockouts or overexpressions) before laboratory implementation [
89
]. Such constraints‐based modelling is a core part of the ‘Design’ phase in the DBTL cycle and is increasingly integrated with machine learning‐driven multiomic analysis to identify biomarkers [
90
] or investigate the cellular state under production conditions [
91
]. The resulting gene targets then inform the ‘Build’ phase (e.g., construct assembly and transformation), followed by ‘Test’ (e.g., LC‐MS validation of metabolic re‐routing) and ‘Learn’ (model retraining), progressively shortening the DBTL loop (Figure
2
).
FIGURE 2
The iterative design‐build‐test‐learn (DBTL) cycle in engineering biology for plant cell line improvement. This workflow guides the rational engineering of plant cell line improvement, starting with multiomics analysis and computational design, followed by precision gene editing, performance (yield) testing and data analysis to inform the next cycle of design.
Multiomics approaches also illuminate upper‐level regulatory networks. Chromatin‐profiling techniques, such as ChIP‐seq, have been used to identify histone modifications (e.g., H3K27me3 [
92
] and variants thereof (e.g., H2A.Z) [
93
]), and these molecular ‘on/off’ switches have been found regulating plant BGC expression. For example, in
Arabidopsis
, the repressive H3K27me3 mark is notably associated with silenced triterpene biosynthetic gene clusters, such as the thalianol cluster, influencing their 3D chromosomal conformation and transcriptional state [
94
]. In PCC, widely used elicitors, such as methyl jasmonate (MeJA) and salicylic acid (SA), can themselves induce chromatin remodelling at defence‐related loci, helping to explain durable shifts in pathway expression during elicitation regimes [
95
]. Thus, incorporating these epigenomic layers into BGC discovery pipelines, such as plantiSMASH [
96
] and PhytoClust [
97
], helps identify silent BGCs, providing potential targets for CRISPR interference, an approach recently demonstrated in
Streptomyces
[
98
].
Such epigenetic data significantly strengthen in silico predictions. Yu et al. demonstrated that combining chromatin signatures with co‐expression analysis significantly enhances the accuracy of delineating and discovering BGCs in plants including
Arabidopsis
, oat and maize [
99
]. Moreover, integrating multiomics with phenomics links intracellular titres to observable culture traits (e.g., aggregate size and shear tolerance), thereby enabling multiobjective optimisation strategies aimed at enhancing both productivity and bioprocess robustness.
3.2
Gene Manipulation and Pathway Bioengineering
Modern plant metabolic engineering has entered an era of precision, enabling single‐nucleotide edits, the insertion of multikilobase pathways and the implementation of synthetic gene circuitry, often as integrated components of the iterative DBTL cycle [
100
,
101
]. Central to this advancement is the versatile CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) toolkit. This toolkit now encompasses nuclease‐mediated gene knockouts for functional analysis or pathway blocking, base editors and prime editors for precise, scar‐free nucleotide conversions without double‐strand breaks and nuclease‐deactivated Cas (dCas) fusions that can be targeted to programme transcriptional or epigenetic states without altering the underlying DNA sequence [
102
].
The practical impact of these gene manipulation tools is evident in numerous recent studies. For instance, in
Nicotiana tabacum
BY‐2 suspension cells, a multiplex CRISPR/Cas9 strategy was successfully employed to simultaneously inactivate two
β(1,2)‐xylosyltransferase
(
XylT
) genes and four
α(1,3)‐fucosyltransferase
(
FucT
) genes, involving the disruption of 12 alleles in total. This glycoengineering effort resulted in strains producing glycoproteins devoid of plant‐specific xylose and fucose residues, crucial for reducing potential immunogenicity of plant‐made biopharmaceuticals [
103
]. Base editing offers an even finer level of control by enabling precise nucleotide conversions without inducing double‐strand breaks. For example, CRISPR‐mediated base editing successfully introduced targeted C‐to‐T mutations in the
CELLULOSE SYNTHASE A3
(
CESA3
) gene in
Arabidopsis thaliana
cell suspension cultures, conferring resistance to the cellulose biosynthesis inhibitor C17 and demonstrating a method to rapidly generate valuable traits or selectable markers directly in cultured cells [
104
]. Furthermore, the challenge of stable transgene integration and segregation in slow‐growing or vegetatively propagated medicinal plants is being addressed by transgene‐free genome editing approaches. The delivery of preassembled Cas9‐sgRNA ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) directly into plant protoplasts, followed by regeneration, has proven effective for generating edited, transgene‐free carrot (
Daucus carota
) plants, a significant advancement for crop improvement and potentially applicable to medicinal plant cell cultures [
105
].
CRISPR technology is increasingly utilised not only to modify gene function by altering coding sequences but also to precisely rewire gene regulation. Nuclease‐deactivated Cas9 (dCas9) fused to transcriptional activator domains (CRISPRa) has been effectively used to upregulate target genes [
106
]. A DNA‐free CRISPR/dCas9‐VP64 activator system, delivered as ribonucleoprotein complexes (RNPs) into
Stevia rebaudiana
protoplasts, successfully activated the endogenous
UGT76G1
gene, which is involved in steviol glycoside biosynthesis, showcasing a potent method for enhancing metabolite production in plant cell cultures [
107
]. Epigenome editing driven by dCas9 fusions, offers further regulatory control. Gallego‐Bartolomé et al. showed that fusing the catalytic domain of the human DNA demethylase TET1 (TET1cd) to dCas9 (via a SunTag system) could precisely target and reverse DNA methylation at specific loci, such as the
FWA
promoter in whole
Arabidopsis thaliana
plants, leading to a heritable late‐flowering phenotype [
108
]. Althouugh such an approach has not been applied to plant cell suspensions yet, the success in whole plants underscores its potential for addressing epigenetic instability and loss of productivity in these culture systems [
109
].
When catalytic bottlenecks within a pathway are caused by enzymes whose structure–function relationships are poorly understood, precise editing and synthetic circuits are increasingly complemented by directed evolution strategies. These strategies aim to improve enzyme characteristics by mimicking natural evolution in the laboratory through iterative cycles of genetic diversification and functional selection or screening [
110
]. Butt et al. utilised a T7 RNA polymerase‐cytidine deaminase fusion for in vivo targeted mutagenesis of the
acetolactate synthase
(
OsALS
) gene in rice. By applying herbicide selection pressure to transgenic rice calli and regenerated plants, they successfully evolved and identified
OsALS
variants conferring herbicide resistance, demonstrating a powerful approach for directed enzyme evolution directly within plant systems [
111
].
These diverse gene manipulation and pathway engineering strategies are most powerful when integrated into rapid DBTL cycles. The semi‐synthetic artemisinin project serves as a landmark example: extensive engineering of yeast was undertaken, including overexpression of the mevalonate pathway (featuring a key truncated HMG‐CoA reductase) and downregulation of the competing squalene synthase to boost farnesyl diphosphate precursor, coupled with the expression and optimisation of the multistep
Artemisia annua
biosynthetic pathway to artemisinic acid (involving amorphadiene oxidase CYP71AV1, its reductase CPR1, cytochrome b5, alcohol dehydrogenase ADH1 and aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH1, often under inducible promoters). These efforts, refined through successive DBTL iterations, led to gram‐scale production of artemisinic acid (up to 25 g/L) in yeast [
112
].
Gene manipulation and pathway bioengineering tools, encompassing precise genome editing, dCas9‐based transcriptional and epigenetic modulation, the assembly of artificial gene clusters, and sophisticated directed evolution strategies, are collectively transforming our ability to engineer plant cells. When integrated within iterative DBTL cycles, these approaches facilitate more rational, efficient and predictable engineering of plant cell metabolism. The capacity to precisely modify genetic sequences, rewire regulatory networks, reconstruct complex biosynthetic pathways and evolve novel enzyme functions, marks a significant advancement over traditional methods. This progress is paving the way for the development of highly optimised plant cell factories capable of producing valuable specialised metabolites at improved yields and with enhanced stability.
3.3
Biosensors for High‐Throughput Screening and Real‐Time Monitoring
The successful application of gene manipulation and pathway refactoring strategies often results in extensive libraries of engineered cell lines or synthetic genetic constructs. To fully harness this genetic diversity, rapid and efficient methods are essential for identifying variants with improved productivity and for monitoring metabolic states during cultivation. Genetically encoded biosensors have become indispensable tools for these purposes [
113
,
114
,
115
]. These molecular devices are engineered to convert the intracellular concentration of a specific analyte, such as a metabolite or hormone, into a readily quantifiable output, typically an optical (e.g., fluorescence and luminescence) or transcriptional signal [
116
]. This output can be measured in living cells, facilitating high‐throughput screening (HTS) of large cell populations via techniques, such as fluorescence‐activated cell sorting (FACS), or monitored continuously for real‐time process control in bioreactors [
113
]. Over the past decade, biosensor design has significantly advanced from simple indirect promoter‐reporter systems to a sophisticated array of reversible, orthogonal and even logic‐gated devices, increasingly tailored with response dynamics suitable for industrial applications and automated detection [
113
,
116
]. As a key component of the ‘Test’ phase in the DBTL cycle, biosensors provide crucial quantitative data that informs the ‘Learn’ phase, thereby accelerating strain improvement.
Early plant biosensing frequently employed indirect transcriptional reporters, such as the auxin‐responsive
DR5
promoter driving Green Fluorescent Protein (GFP) expression [
117
] or the cytokinin‐responsive TCSn promoter linked to Venus [
118
,
119
]. Although valuable for mapping hormone signalling, these reporters were often limited by slow reporter maturation and potential pathway crosstalk [
116
]. Newer generations of direct biosensors, particularly those based on Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET), have overcome many of these issues. For example, FRET‐based auxin sensors (e.g., AuxSen) and abscisic acid sensors (e.g., ABAleon2.1 and ABACUS1‐2µ) provide rapid and reversible readouts of hormone dynamics with high spatiotemporal resolution [
120
,
121
,
122
]. Degradation‐based reporters, such as DII‐VENUS for auxin [
123
] and Jas9‐VENUS for jasmonate [
124
], offer alternative strategies for monitoring hormone levels by linking hormone presence to reporter protein degradation.
Beyond hormone sensing, protein engineering has enabled the creation of orthogonal ligand‐inducible switches (Figure
3
). For instance, a mutated ABA receptor (
PYR1
*
MANDI
) was engineered to bind the fungicide mandipropamid instead of ABA, creating an externally controllable switch for gene expression in plants [
125
]. Transcription factor (TF)‐based biosensors, often derived from bacterial regulators, represent another versatile class. The TtgR repressor, for example, responds to the flavonoid naringenin and has been engineered into AND logic gates for more precise control over metabolic pathways [
126
,
127
]. Such TF‐based biosensors are valuable for screening high‐producing strains and for dynamic pathway regulation [
127
].
FIGURE 3
Illustration of two bioengineering approaches in biosensor design. (A) A chemically induced dimerisation system, exemplified by the plant‐derived PYR/HAB system, where receptor proteins are fused to fragments of a split‐reporter. In the absence of a ligand, the fragments remain separate and inactive. Upon ligand binding, the receptor complex assembles, bringing the reporter fragments into close proximity and generating a measurable signal. (B) Transcription factor‐based biosensor, exemplified by the bacterial TtgR system (repressor), to control gene expression. The repressor actively binds to DNA, blocking transcription of a reporter gene. When a ligand binds to the repressor, it causes it to release from the DNA, enabling reporter expression.
Integrating biosensors with CRISPR‐based regulatory elements can forge sophisticated, highly orthogonal control circuits. For instance, by engineering reprogrammed trans‐acting CRISPR RNAs (tracrRNAs), Cas9 can be directed to utilise endogenous cellular RNAs (such as mRNAs or small RNAs) as CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs). This strategy enables the direct sensing of cellular transcriptional states, linking them to downstream CRISPR‐mediated gene regulation or reporting, and thereby offers a pathway to designing feedback loops for autonomous control of metabolic pathways [
128
]. Novel biosensor architectures, including dimerisation‐dependent fluorescent proteins [
129
] and split‐luciferase systems [
130
], along with computational design and directed evolution of sensor proteins [
131
], continue to broaden the scope and applicability of biosensor technology.
Ultimately, biosensors are more than just reporters; they are active components in the engineering cycle, providing quantitative data that feeds into predictive models and reveals cellular heterogeneity [
116
,
127
]. For example, Häkkinen et al. [
132
] used a fluorescent reporter (GFP–HFBI) to isolate homogeneous
Nicotiana tabacum
BY‐2 clones and then tracked expression over 19 passages, demonstrating that fluorescence‐guided subcloning plus longitudinal monitoring can be used to detect and manage cell‐line instability while maintaining gram‐per‐litre yields. This evolution towards data‐driven sensor‐guided engineering is paving the way for self‐optimising plant cell factories, where metabolic performance is continuously monitored and autonomously adjusted. The maturation of biosensor technology represents a critical advance for realising the full potential of plant‐based biomanufacturing.
4
Concluding Remarks
The integration of multiomics‐driven design, precision genome and pathway engineering,and advanced biosensor‐guided monitoring within the iterative DBTL cycle is revolutionising plant cell culture technology. This synergistic framework propels the field beyond traditional empirical methods, establishing a rational, predictable and highly efficient paradigm for creating superior plant cell factories.
Despite these significant strides, persistent challenges require ongoing innovation. Crucially, the predictive power of in silico models must be enhanced by integrating complex regulatory data such as epigenetics. The efficiency of the ‘Build’ phase also needs improvement, especially concerning multiplex genome editing in intricate plant genomes and the assembly of large‐scale genetic constructs, to expedite development. Moreover, the ‘Test’ and ‘Learn’ phases will benefit immensely from an expanded and more robust toolkit of biosensors, particularly those optimised for the demanding conditions of in planta applications.
Nevertheless, the forward trajectory is undeniable. The DBTL framework, continually energised by advancements across its core components, facilitates increasingly rapid and potent optimisation of plant cell lines. The capacity to quantitatively design metabolic engineering strategies, accurately implement them cellularly, rigorously test their impacts and iteratively learn from these outcomes is already delivering significant gains in bioactive compound yields and production efficiency.
The potential benefit to industrial plant cell culture applications is encouraging. Future developments will likely feature highly automated platforms where federated learning refines predictive models, sophisticated epigenetic editors offer precise control over gene expression and advanced microfluidics integrated with next‐generation biosensors enable ultra‐high‐throughput screening and selection of elite strains. The ultimate aspiration is the realisation of self‐optimising plant cell factories: intelligent cyber‐physical systems capable of continuous self‐monitoring and autonomous adjustment of metabolic processes to achieve and sustain peak performance and stability.
The integrated application of engineering biology's powerful toolkit, orchestrated within the DBTL cycle, is decisively unlocking the immense potential of plant cell cultures. This ongoing transformation is poised to deliver sustainable, scalable and economically viable bio‐foundries. These advanced cellular systems will serve as a crucial source for a diverse array of valuable plant‐derived molecules—spanning pharmaceuticals, functional foods and green chemicals—thus making a significant contribution to a burgeoning biobased economy with a substantially reduced ecological footprint.
